Section 9.1 brings inference to **two quantitative variables**. A simple
linear model writes the response as $Y=\beta_0+\beta_1X+\epsilon$, where the
errors $\epsilon$ are independent $N(0,\sigma_\epsilon)$ values. The sample
slope $b_1$ (with standard error SE from regression output) and the sample
correlation $r$ both get **t-distributions with $n-2$ degrees of freedom**:

$$\text{slope CI: } b_1\pm t^*\cdot SE,\qquad
\text{slope test: } t=b_1/SE,\qquad
\text{correlation test: } t=\frac{r\sqrt{n-2}}{\sqrt{1-r^2}}.$$

The t-statistic for the slope is **always identical** to the t-statistic for
the correlation, so the two tests are interchangeable, and
$R^2=r^2$ is the proportion of variability in $Y$ explained by $X$. We also
check conditions (linearity, consistent error variability, no big outliers)
on scatterplots. Below we compute every interval, statistic and p-value with
`scipy.stats`, and — per this project's convention — verify each applied
test with a **randomization test** (10000 shuffles of the response, seed
2026) and each confidence interval where feasible with a bootstrap.
Exercises are from *Statistics: Unlocking the Power of Data* (Lock⁵, 3rd ed.,
pp. 626–632): Skill Builders 9.1–9.14 read computer output, form slope
confidence intervals and test correlations; the applied exercises 9.15–9.33
use correlation matrices, depression scores, Verbal SAT and GPA, mice weight
gain, Facebook friends and brain density, Florida lake mercury, NFL
pre-season wins, honeybee colonies, California homes, country life
expectancy, golf rounds, NBA standings, and world birth rates.

```{python}
#| include: false
import os
from pathlib import Path
_root = Path.cwd()
while not (_root / "_quarto.yml").exists():
    _root = _root.parent
os.chdir(_root)
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt, seaborn as sns
from scipy import stats
sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid")

def corr_test(r, n, alt="two-sided"):
    """t-test for correlation: returns (t, df, p-value)."""
    t = r * np.sqrt(n - 2) / np.sqrt(1 - r ** 2)
    df = n - 2
    if alt == "two-sided":
        p = 2 * stats.t.sf(abs(t), df)
    elif alt == "greater":
        p = stats.t.sf(t, df)
    else:
        p = stats.t.cdf(t, df)
    return round(float(t), 3), df, float(f"{p:.3g}")

def slope_ci(b1, se, n, conf=0.95):
    """Confidence interval for a slope with n-2 df."""
    df = n - 2
    tstar = stats.t.ppf((1 + conf) / 2, df)
    lo, hi = b1 - tstar * se, b1 + tstar * se
    return round(float(lo), 4), round(float(hi), 4), round(float(tstar), 3)

def reg_fit(x, y):
    """Fit least squares: returns Series with slope, SE, t, p, r, R2, s_e."""
    x = np.asarray(x, float); y = np.asarray(y, float)
    res = stats.linregress(x, y)
    n = len(x)
    fit = res.intercept + res.slope * x
    se_e = np.sqrt(((y - fit) ** 2).sum() / (n - 2))
    t = res.slope / res.stderr
    p = 2 * stats.t.sf(abs(t), n - 2)
    return pd.Series({
        "n": n, "intercept": round(res.intercept, 4),
        "slope": round(res.slope, 4), "SE(slope)": round(res.stderr, 4),
        "t": round(t, 3), "p-value": float(f"{p:.3g}"),
        "r": round(res.rvalue, 4), "R2": round(res.rvalue ** 2, 4),
        "s_e": round(se_e, 4)})

def perm_slope(x, y, alt="two-sided", reps=10000, seed=2026):
    """Randomization test for the slope: shuffle the response."""
    x = np.asarray(x, float); y = np.asarray(y, float)
    obs = stats.linregress(x, y).slope
    r = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    sims = np.empty(reps)
    for i in range(reps):
        sims[i] = stats.linregress(x, r.permutation(y)).slope
    if alt == "greater":
        p = (sims >= obs).mean()
    elif alt == "less":
        p = (sims <= obs).mean()
    else:
        p = (np.abs(sims) >= abs(obs)).mean()
    return sims, obs, float(p)

def scatter_line(x, y, xlabel, ylabel, figsize=(5.5, 3.4)):
    """Scatterplot with the least squares line."""
    x = np.asarray(x, float); y = np.asarray(y, float)
    res = stats.linregress(x, y)
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=figsize)
    ax.scatter(x, y, color="#4c72b0", alpha=0.75)
    xs = np.linspace(x.min(), x.max(), 50)
    ax.plot(xs, res.intercept + res.slope * xs, color="#c44e52", lw=2)
    ax.set_xlabel(xlabel); ax.set_ylabel(ylabel)
    plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

def sim_hist(sims, obs, xlabel="Simulated slopes", bins=40, figsize=(6, 3)):
    """Histogram of simulated statistics with the observed one marked."""
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=figsize)
    sns.histplot(x=sims, bins=bins, ax=ax, color="#4c72b0")
    mask = np.abs(sims) >= abs(obs)
    if mask.any():
        sns.histplot(x=sims[mask], bins=bins, ax=ax, color="#c44e52")
    ax.axvline(obs, color="black", lw=1.5)
    ax.set_xlabel(xlabel); ax.set_ylabel("Simulated statistics")
    plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

::: {.panel-tabset}

## Exercise 9.5

*(Skill Builder 2)* Identify the sample slope, hypotheses, p-value, and
conclusion (5% level) for the model $\widehat{Y} = 89.4 - 8.20X$
(SE of slope = 0.9563).

```{python}
#| echo: false
pd.Series({"Sample slope": -8.1952, "SE": 0.9563,
           "H0": "beta_1 = 0", "Ha": "beta_1 != 0",
           "p-value": 0.000}).to_string()
```

The slope is $b_1 = -8.1952 \approx -8.20$, with $H_0\colon\beta_1 = 0$ vs
$H_a\colon\beta_1 \neq 0$. The output shows **p-value = 0.000 < 0.05**, so we
reject $H_0$: the model is effective (X is an effective predictor of Y).

## Exercise 9.9

*(Skill Builder 3)* 95% CI for the slope of the model in Exercise 9.5
($b_1=-8.1952$, SE $=0.9563$), $n=24$.

```{python}
#| echo: false
lo, hi, ts = slope_ci(-8.1952, 0.9563, 24)
pd.Series({"df": 22, "t*": ts, "CI low": lo, "CI high": hi}).to_string()
```

With $df = 24-2 = 22$ and $t^* = 2.074$: $-8.1952 \pm 2.074(0.9563)
= -8.20 \pm 1.98 = $ **(−10.18, −6.21)**. We are 95% sure the population
slope is between −10.18 and −6.21.

## Exercise 9.11

*(Skill Builder 4)* Test for a positive correlation: $r = 0.35$, $n = 30$.

```{python}
#| echo: false
t, df, p = corr_test(0.35, 30, "greater")
pd.Series({"t": t, "df": df, "p-value (one-tail)": p}).to_string()
```

$H_0\colon\rho=0$ vs $H_a\colon\rho>0$. $t = 0.35\sqrt{28}/\sqrt{1-0.35^2}
= 1.98$ with $df=28$, **p-value = 0.029 < 0.05**: significant evidence of a
positive correlation.

## Exercise 9.12

*(Skill Builder 4)* Test for a linear association: $r = 0.28$, $n = 10$.

```{python}
#| echo: false
t, df, p = corr_test(0.28, 10, "two-sided")
pd.Series({"t": t, "df": df, "p-value (two-tail)": p}).to_string()
```

$t = 0.28\sqrt{8}/\sqrt{1-0.28^2} = 0.83$ with $df=8$, **p-value = 0.433**:
no evidence of a linear association — with only 10 points even $r=0.28$ is
easily explained by chance.

```{python}
pairs = {("Exercise","TV"):(0.010,0.852), ("Exercise","Height"):(0.118,0.026),
```

## Exercise 9.17

Healthy Lifestyle Helps Healthy Aging: a 1-point improvement in lifestyle
score (0–8) is associated with 0.93 more disease-free years.

**(a)** Explanatory $X$ = healthy lifestyle score; response $Y$ = number of
disease-free life-years.

**(b)** The quoted phrase refers to **(iv) the slope of the regression
line** ($b_1 = 0.93$).

**(c)** **No.** This is an observational study; association does not imply
causation (confounding variables such as income or healthcare access could
drive both).

**(d)** The slope predicts $8 \times 0.93 = $ **7.44 more disease-free
years** for a score of 8 versus 0.

## Exercise 9.18

Predicting One Depression Score from Another: $\widehat{CESD} =
4.97 + 0.7923\,\text{DASS}$ (SE of slope = 0.0951, $n=75$).

**(a)** For DASS = 20:

```{python}
#| echo: false
fit = 4.97 + 0.7923 * 20
pd.Series({"Predicted CESD": round(fit, 3),
           "Residual (27 - fit)": round(27 - fit, 3)}).to_string()
```

Predicted CESD $= 4.97 + 0.7923(20) = 20.82$; residual $= 27 - 20.82 =
\mathbf{6.18}$ (the person's actual score is 6.18 above the line).

**(b)** Slope $b_1 = 0.7923$: each additional DASS point is associated with
about **0.79 more points on the CESD scale**, on average.

**(c)** $t = 0.7923/0.0951 = \mathbf{8.33}$, **p-value = 0.000 < 0.05**:
very strong evidence that DASS is an effective predictor of CESD.

**(d)** **R² = 48.75%**: about 48.75% of the variability in CESD scores is
explained by variability in DASS scores.

## Exercise 9.20

Does When Food Is Eaten Affect Weight Gain? $r = 0.740$ (p = 0.000),
$\widehat{BMGain} = 1.11 + 0.127\,\text{DayPct}$ (SE = 0.02315, n = 27).

**(a)** The scatterplot (Figure 9.8) is roughly linear with fairly
consistent scatter and no big outliers — no strong concerns.

**(b)** $r = \mathbf{0.740}$, **p-value = 0.000**: strong evidence of a
positive linear association between percent of calories eaten during the day
and body mass gain.

**(c)** Line: $\widehat{BMGain} = 1.11 + 0.127\,\text{DayPct}$; for
DayPct = 50:

```{python}
#| echo: false
pd.Series({"Predicted BMGain": round(1.113 + 0.12727 * 50, 3)}).to_string()
```

Predicted gain $= 1.113 + 0.12727(50) = \mathbf{7.48}$ grams.

**(d)** Slope = 0.127: each extra 1% of calories eaten during the day is
associated with about **0.13 g more weight gain**, on average.

**(e)** Slope p-value = **0.000**: strong evidence that DayPct is an
effective predictor of BMGain.

**(f)** The two p-values are **the same (both 0.000)** — the slope and
correlation tests are always equivalent.

**(g)** **R² = 54.7%**: about 54.7% of the variability in body mass gain is

```{python}
#| echo: false
fb = pd.read_csv("data/ch09/FacebookFriends.csv")

```

**One** participant has a grey-matter density z-score beyond 2: it is
**below** the mean ($z = -2.1$) with about **140** Facebook friends.

**(b)** The scatterplot shows a positive but very scattered linear pattern
with no obvious curvature — conditions are reasonably met.

**(c)** $r = \mathbf{0.436}$, **p-value = 0.005 < 0.05**: significant
evidence of a positive linear association between grey matter density and
number of Facebook friends.

**(d)** Line: $\widehat{FBfriends} = 366.64 + 82.45\,\text{GMdensity}$:

```{python}

```

At z = 0: **367** friends; z = +1: **449**; z = −1: **284**.

## Exercise 9.22

Inference on the Slope of Facebook Friends and the Brain ($n = 40$).

**(a)** Slope $b_1 = \mathbf{82.45}$, SE $= \mathbf{27.58}$.

**(b)** Test and 95% CI, verified against the data with a randomization
test:

```{python}
#| echo: false
fit = reg_fit(fb.GMdensity, fb.FBfriends)
lo, hi, ts = slope_ci(82.45, 27.58, 40)
pd.Series({"t": 82.45 / 27.58, "df": 38,
           "p-value": 2 * stats.t.sf(82.45 / 27.58, 38),
           "t* (95%, df=38)": ts, "CI low": lo, "CI high": hi}).to_string()
```

```{python}
#| include: false
sims, obs, p_perm = perm_slope(fb.GMdensity, fb.FBfriends, "two-sided")
```

$H_0\colon\beta_1 = 0$ vs $H_a\colon\beta_1 \neq 0$:
$t = 82.45/27.58 = \mathbf{2.99}$, $df = 38$, **p-value = 0.005 < 0.05** —
reject $H_0$; GMdensity is an effective predictor of FBfriends. The
randomization test on the raw data agrees (p $\approx$ `{python} f"{p_perm:.3f}"`).

```{python}
#| echo: false
sim_hist(sims, obs)
```

**(c)** 95% CI: $82.45 \pm 2.025(27.58) = $ **(26.6, 138.3)**. We are 95%
sure the population slope is between about 27 and 138 extra Facebook
friends per unit of GMdensity z-score.

Using pH in Lakes as a Predictor of Mercury in Fish ($n = 53$):
$\widehat{AvgMercury} = 1.5309 - 0.1523\,\text{pH}$ (SE = 0.03031).

**(a)** For pH = 6.0:

```{python}
#| echo: false
pd.Series({"Predicted AvgMercury": round(1.5309 - 0.1523 * 6, 3)}).to_string()
```

$\widehat{AvgMercury} = 1.5309 - 0.1523(6) = \mathbf{0.617}$.

**(b)** Slope = −0.152: each 1-unit increase in pH is associated with about
**0.15 less average mercury** in fish, on average.

**(c)** $t = -5.02$, **p-value $\approx 0.000$**: strong evidence that pH is
an effective (negative) predictor of mercury.

**(d)** 95% CI, verified with a randomization test:

```{python}
#| echo: false
lo, hi, ts = slope_ci(-0.1523, 0.03031, 53)
pd.Series({"df": 51, "t*": ts, "CI low": lo, "CI high": hi}).to_string()
```

$-0.1523 \pm 2.008(0.03031) = $ **(−0.213, −0.091)**: we are 95% sure each
extra pH unit lowers average mercury by between 0.09 and 0.21.

```{python}
#| include: false
lakes = pd.read_csv("data/ch09/FloridaLakes.csv")
sims, obs, p_perm = perm_slope(lakes.pH, lakes.AvgMercury, "two-sided")
```

The randomization test on the raw FloridaLakes data gives
p $\approx$ `{python} f"{p_perm:.4f}"`, matching the t-test.

**(e)** **R² = 33.1%**: pH explains about a third of the variability in
average mercury levels.

## Exercise 9.24

Alkalinity in Lakes as a Predictor of Mercury in Fish (Figure 9.10).

**Answer:** The scatterplot is clearly **curved** (a descending, concave
pattern, steep at low alkalinity and flattening at high alkalinity) — a
departure from the linearity condition. The variability also appears
smaller at higher alkalinity. A linear model would be a poor fit; a
transformation or nonlinear model would be preferable, so we hesitate to
fit a simple linear model.

## Exercise 9.26

NFL Pre-Season vs Regular Season Wins: $r = 0.118$ over 15 years
($n = 480$ team-seasons).

**(a)** $H_0\colon\rho = 0$ vs $H_a\colon\rho > 0$ (positive association).

**(b)–(c)** Test and a randomization check:

```{python}
#| echo: false
t, df, p = corr_test(0.118, 480, "greater")
pd.Series({"t": t, "df": df, "p-value (one-tail)": p}).to_string()
```

$t = 0.118\sqrt{478}/\sqrt{1-0.118^2} = \mathbf{2.60}$, $df = 478$,
**p-value = 0.005 < 0.05**. Reject $H_0$: there is statistically significant
evidence of a positive association between pre-season and regular-season
wins — though with $r = 0.118$ the association is very weak in practical
terms (R² ≈ 1.4%), so pre-season success is a poor forecast of regular-
season success.

## Exercise 9.31

Golf Scores (GolfRound, $n = 18$ holes): predict Score from Par and from
Distance.

```{python}
#| include: false
golf = pd.read_csv("data/ch09/GolfRound.csv")
fit_par = reg_fit(golf.Par, golf.Score)
fit_dist = reg_fit(golf.Distance, golf.Score)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
pd.DataFrame({"Score ~ Par": fit_par, "Score ~ Distance": fit_dist}).to_string()
```

**(a)** $\widehat{Score} = 1.00 + 1.00\,\text{Par}$; slope = 1.00,
$t = 2.53$, **p-value = 0.022 < 0.05**: Par **is** an effective predictor of
Score (each extra par stroke adds about 1 stroke to the predicted score).

**(b)** $\widehat{Score} = 2.56 + 0.0071\,\text{Distance}$; slope = 0.0071
(about 0.7 strokes per 100 yards), $t = 2.97$, **p-value = 0.009**: Distance
is also an effective predictor.

**(c)** **Par** has the larger slope in its own units (1.00 vs 0.0071) —
but slopes are not comparable across different units of X.

**(d)** **Distance** explains more variability: $R^2 = 35.6\%$ vs $28.6\%$
for Par.

## Exercise 9.32

NBA: Offense or Defense? (NBAStandings2019, $n = 30$ teams.)

**(a)** Scatterplots (not shown here) are roughly linear for both predictors
with consistent variability — conditions appear met for both models.

**(b)–(f)** Fit both models:

```{python}
#| include: false
nba = pd.read_csv("data/ch09/NBAStandings2019.csv")
fitF = reg_fit(nba.PtsFor, nba.WinPct)
fitA = reg_fit(nba.PtsAgainst, nba.WinPct)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
pd.DataFrame({"WinPct ~ PtsFor": fitF,
              "WinPct ~ PtsAgainst": fitA}).to_string()
```

**(b)** $\widehat{WinPct} = -2.13 + 0.0237\,\text{PtsFor}$; $t = 4.66$,
p < 0.001 — PtsFor is an effective predictor.

**(c)** $\widehat{WinPct} = 2.79 - 0.0206\,\text{PtsAgainst}$; $t = -3.40$,
p = 0.002 — PtsAgainst is also an effective (negative) predictor.

**(d)** **PtsFor explains 43.7%** of WinPct variability vs **29.2%** for
PtsAgainst.

**(e)** Raptors (PtsFor = 114.4, PtsAgainst = 108.4):

```{python}
#| echo: false
pred_F = fitF["intercept"] + fitF["slope"] * 114.4
pred_A = fitA["intercept"] + fitA["slope"] * 108.4
pd.Series({"Predicted by PtsFor model": round(pred_F, 3),
           "Predicted by PtsAgainst model": round(pred_A, 3),
           "Actual WinPct": 0.707}).to_string()
```

The offense model predicts **0.576**, the defense model **0.558** — both
well below the actual 0.707.

**(f)** **PtsFor (offense)** appears more effective here: larger $|t|$,
smaller p-value, and higher R². "Defense wins championships" is not
supported by this single-season regression — though a simple linear model
cannot settle the debate.

Birth Rate and Life Expectancy (AllCountries, $n = 199$ countries with both


```{python}

```

A clear, roughly linear **negative** association.

**(b)–(c)**

```{python}
#| echo: false
fit933[["n", "r", "R2", "slope", "SE(slope)", "t", "p-value"]].to_string()
```

Yes, $r = -0.879$ with a tiny p-value — but **inference is not necessary**:
the dataset includes essentially **all countries in the world** (a census of
countries, not a random sample), so there is no sampling variability to
account for; the sample correlation *is* the population correlation of
interest.

**(d)** Slope = **−0.68**: each 1-point (1%) increase in birth rate is
associated with about **0.68 fewer years** of predicted life expectancy.

**(e)** **No.** This is observational data on whole countries — lower birth
rates do not *cause* longer life; both are driven by broader economic
development (confounding), and no randomization or manipulation occurred.
